overview: Later Tang was a short-lived northern Chinese dynasty founded by Li Cunxu in 923. Its Shatuo-led ruling network claimed the prestige of the earlier Tang, but was a separate regime. The map’s 923-937 interval and coarse outline simplify changing control, military governorships and rival states; they do not describe a reunited China.

periods.title: Conquest and a fragile court
periods.summary: Li Cunxu defeated Later Liang, but military success failed to secure a stable reign.

periods.title: Mingzong’s consolidation
periods.summary: Li Siyuan worked with civil and military advisers to stabilize government and restrain expenditure.

periods.title: Succession and overthrow
periods.summary: Contested successions ended with Shi Jingtang’s rebellion, Khitan intervention and the last emperor’s death in January 937.

sections.title: A new dynasty using an old name

items.text: Li Cunxu’s power grew from the northern military world of his father, Li Keyong. Shatuo leaders worked with people of several backgrounds, including Sogdian, Uighur and Chinese connections. The family’s granted Li surname helped its claim to carry on the earlier Tang’s authority.

Li Cunxu conquered Later Liang in 923, ruled from Luoyang and sent an army that captured Chengdu in 925. Disgruntled soldiers brought his reign to a violent end in 926. Winning battles and keeping troops supplied, paid and loyal were different jobs. His successor Li Siyuan became Emperor Mingzong.

Mingzong cultivated cooperation with civilian advisers and military commanders, reduced waste and directed revenue toward the public treasury. Historian Richard Davis presents his reign as a period of relative stability, while also noting its harsh punishments. Effective management did not mean gentle government.

Military families could be made through adoption as well as birth. Li Keyong recruited skilled fighters as surrogate sons, and Mingzong himself entered his household as an adopted youth. Such relationships helped build armies, but disputes between sons and brothers also made succession dangerous.

Women in the ruling household could advise and teach. Before Later Tang’s founding, Li Keyong’s wife Lady Liu trained household women in riding and archery. Under Mingzong, Empress Cao and Consort Wang supported one another at court. These are particular elite lives, not a rule for every woman.

A 929 edict preserved in a later institutional compilation required farming households to report their planted acreage, with groups of five households guaranteeing the declarations. Local officials were forbidden to send inspectors to remeasure it. Fields were both a family livelihood and a subject of government paperwork.

The same compilation records a 931 order that military farms should recruit unattached migrants and cultivate ownerless wasteland, rather than draw registered taxpayers away from their home counties. Rival demands for workers could reach straight into village life.

An early Song collection tells of Mingzong sharing a drink made with poppy seeds with commanders during a supply shortage. A modern historian examines it as food history. This later anecdote offers a glimpse of making do during campaigning, not an everyday menu for the whole population.

After the change of ruler in 926, the imperial kitchen staff was cut to fifty. Even the reduced royal kitchen was a substantial workplace! The recorded cut shows how court luxury depended on many workers, and why palace expenses became a political issue.

sections.title: A tomb that preserves a furnished world

items.text: Wang Chuzhi’s tomb at Quyang in Hebei, dated to 924, preserves an elite world formed before Later Tang. Its carved and painted decoration and buried epitaph survived despite robbery. Wang’s career crossed the earlier Tang and Five Dynasties transition; the tomb is not an emperor’s palace.

A relief from the tomb depicts fifteen figures, including musicians, a conductor and dancers. Excavated in 1995, it gives researchers an unusually detailed picture of performance. The stone cannot play the tune, but the performers’ instruments and arrangement preserve clues to how an ensemble worked.

Painted furnishings include tall folding screens, a three-part screen, an almost square screen and low horizontal ones. Art historian Jonathan Hay uses these images to study room decoration. A screen could be furniture and a place for pictures at once, bringing painted scenery into an elite interior.

The tomb’s epitaph and later official biographies do not agree about the family position of Wang Du, Wang Chuzhi’s successor. Comparing them reveals how families and historians shaped reputations. An inscription is valuable evidence, but praising the deceased was part of its job.

Shanghai Museum holds a cast copper Tiancheng yuanbao coin from Mingzong’s Tiancheng reign. It is just 23.66 millimetres across and carries regular-script characters. The museum records it as a donation by Sun Ding, so its catalogue does not establish an excavated household context.

The coin’s legend is 天成元寶, read in modern Mandarin as tiānchéng yuánbǎo: literally, “original treasure of the Tiancheng era,” a currency title. These are modern printed forms of the attested Chinese characters, not a reproduction of the casting; the pronunciation is modern, too.

A change of ruler did not empty everyone’s purse. The Bank of Japan’s Currency Museum explains that earlier Tang Kaiyuan coins continued circulating under the northern Five Dynasties, whose own minting was often limited. Old coins could outlast the government that issued them.

Under Later Tang, Feng Dao promoted a government project to print the Confucian Classics with carved wooden blocks. The Directorate of Education used earlier Tang stone inscriptions as models. The achievement was organized editing and reproduction of authoritative texts; private woodblock printing already existed.

Those Five Dynasties editions have been lost, according to the National Palace Museum. Surviving later books help trace their influence, but the museum’s illustrated Mencius volume is a Southern Song edition. A photograph of an old book is not automatically a photograph of the first edition!

ending.text: Shi Jingtang rebelled with Khitan assistance in 936, and Later Tang collapsed as Later Jin took power. The last emperor’s reign ended in January 937, explaining the map’s endpoint. The ruling house lost the throne; communities, officials, books and earlier monetary traditions continued under new political arrangements.
